scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether pulling a sickie to go to a job interview is right or wrong. Let me start by understanding the situation better. The person is a nurse who has been working in a community hospital. Initially, she loved her job, but over time, the unit has become more of a free care home for patients who can't go home but also can't stay in the hospital. This has led to a lot of stress because they're dealing with patients who have cognitive and behavioral issues, which they aren't really trained for. Plus, her boss is really awful, always finding faults and being demoralizing. She's been taking this because her sickness level has been high, dealing with chronic depression and anxiety. She's been interviewing for other jobs but has had to go after night shifts, which is exhausting. She feels like this has negatively affected her chances of getting a new job. She's about to have another interview and can't face doing another night shift before it. She worked 40 hours already this week, and the idea of another shift plus the interview made her break down in tears. She called in sick with a headache and feels guilty. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for her to pull a sickie to go to the interview? First, I need to consider the ethical implications. On one hand, she's taking a sick day when she's not actually sick, which could be seen as dishonest. On the other hand, she's in a really tough situation where her mental health is suffering, and she needs to secure a better job to improve her well-being. I should also think about the impact on her workplace. If she calls in sick, someone else has to cover her shift, which might put extra strain on her colleagues. But at the same time, she's been working long hours and needs a break to take care of herself. Another angle is the importance of self-care. She's dealing with chronic depression and anxiety, and working under such stressful conditions isn't sustainable. Taking a day off to focus on her mental health and to increase her chances of getting a better job could be seen as a responsible decision. However, there's also the issue of honesty. If she's not actually sick, is it fair to her employer to take a sick day? Employers generally expect employees to be honest about their reasons for taking time off. Misusing sick days could lead to trust issues in the workplace. But then again, if her mental health is deteriorating to the point where she can't function properly, maybe taking a day off is necessary, regardless of the reason. Some workplaces have policies for mental health days, which are similar to sick days but specifically for mental well-being. I also need to consider the long-term consequences. If she continues to work in this toxic environment without seeking a better job, her health could get worse, affecting not just her job performance but her personal life as well. By taking a sick day to go to an interview, she's taking a proactive step towards improving her situation. On the flip side, if she's found out that she took a sick day for an interview, it could damage her reputation at her current job, and she might face disciplinary action. But if she's planning to leave anyway, maybe the risk is worth it. Overall, it seems like a tough call. There are valid arguments on both sides. It's important to weigh the immediate benefits of taking a sick day to secure a better job against the potential long-term consequences of dishonesty and the impact on her current workplace. Maybe she could explore other options first, like discussing her workload or mental health concerns with her employer, or seeing if the interview can be rescheduled. If those aren't possible, then taking a sick day might be the only way for her to move forward. In conclusion, while pulling a sickie isn't ideal, in this specific situation where her mental health and well-being are at risk, and she's actively seeking a better job, it might be justified as a necessary step to improve her circumstances.
